title: Whose Side Is This?
theme: Bias and perspective: how a source shapes what you see
objectives: I can describe how a source can slant the facts by choosing, leaving out, or arranging them.
I can use words like partisan, agenda, and allegiance to ask who is speaking and what that speaker wants.
I can explain how selective details and omitted facts can skew a reader's perception.
I can use the endings -ive, -al, and -ation to understand and build related words.
rationale: Once students can name nuance, they can ask who is speaking and what has been left out. This unit gives them words for the three levers of bias: what a source chooses to include (selective, slant), what it leaves out (omit, skew), and what the speaker wants (agenda, allegiance, partisan, manipulate). Perception and controversial name the reader's side of the exchange: what the audience ends up believing and why a topic divides people. The scenario is a media-class comparison of two reports on the same event, a routine students will repeat with news, ads, and social media. Slant, skew, and agenda each have an everyday meaning that students already know, so the unit teaches the evaluative sense on purpose.

words.def: A way of presenting information that favors one side over another.

senses.def: A slope or tilt, as of a line or surface.
senses.example: The roof has a steep slant so that snow slides off.

words.ex: The editorial's slant was clear from its first sentence, which called the other side's plan reckless.
words.ex2: Compare how two news sites describe the same speech, and you can often detect a slant in the verbs they choose.
words.nonExample: A report that gives each side equal space and equally careful wording has no slant.

apps.academic: To spot a slant, underline the loaded verbs and adjectives and ask what the writer would have said about the other side.
apps.spoken: I think that article has a slant; it only quotes people who agree with the writer.
apps.writing: Use slant for the overall lean of a piece of writing; point to specific word choices as proof.

cloze.s: The ___ of the article was clear: every expert it quoted agreed with the writer, and every critic was called angry.

cloze2.s: Reporters try to remove any ___ from the news by checking their word choices for loaded language.

misuse.s: Her report had no slant at all, since it praised one team in every line and ignored the other.
misuse.why: Slant means favoring one side; praising only one team is exactly that.

visual.alt: A newspaper page tilting toward one side.

words.frame: The slant of this source is ___ because ___.

words.def: Strongly loyal to one side, group, or party, and unfair to the others.
words.ex: The partisan crowd booed every call that went against the home team.
words.ex2: A partisan website tends to praise one political party and ignore the other's good ideas.
words.nonExample: A judge who weighs both sides equally is not partisan.

apps.academic: Historians check whether a newspaper from the past was partisan before they use it as evidence about an election.
apps.spoken: Don't be so partisan; the other team made a good play too.
apps.writing: Use partisan to describe a person, group, or source that supports one side without fairness to others.

cloze.s: The ___ newsletter praised the mayor in every issue and never mentioned a single complaint.

cloze2.s: Because the committee was split along ___ lines, nobody expected the two camps to agree on anything.

misuse.s: The referee was partisan because she treated both teams in exactly the same way.
misuse.why: A partisan person favors one side; treating both sides equally is the opposite.

visual.alt: Fans in matching jerseys cheering loudly in a stadium.

words.frame: A partisan source supports ___ and tends to ignore ___.

words.def: A purpose that a person or group is quietly or openly trying to promote.

senses.def: A list of items to be discussed or done at a meeting.
senses.example: The first item on the agenda was the school budget.

words.ex: The article claimed to be neutral, but its hidden agenda was to sell more of the company's phones.
words.ex2: Before you accept an ad's claim, ask what agenda sits behind it.
words.nonExample: A weather forecast that simply describes tomorrow's sky has no agenda beyond informing you.
words.rel: what a speaker is trying to achieve

apps.academic: Every author has an agenda; analysis begins by asking whether it is stated or hidden.
apps.spoken: I'm not sure what her agenda is, but she keeps steering the conversation back to money.
apps.writing: Use agenda for a goal that shapes what a writer includes; the word often suggests the goal is not announced.

cloze.s: The columnist never admitted her ___, but every example she chose pushed readers toward voting for the same candidate.

cloze2.s: At the meeting, everyone claimed to want what was best for the school, yet each speaker's ___ became obvious when the talk turned to money.

misuse.s: She had no agenda, so she planned every word of her speech to push the audience toward one particular choice.
misuse.why: An agenda is a goal someone is promoting; carefully steering an audience shows one.

visual.alt: A clipboard with a magnifying glass revealing a note written in the margin.

words.frame: I think the agenda behind this is ___ because ___.

words.def: To twist or distort information so that it gives a false or one-sided picture.

senses.def: To lie or move at a slant or angle.
senses.example: The cheap shelf began to skew to one side after a month.

words.ex: Leaving out the rainy weeks can skew a report about the town's climate.
words.ex2: Surveys that reach only people who already like a product will skew the results.
words.nonExample: Measuring every student, not just the tallest ones, keeps an average height from being skewed.

apps.academic: Researchers check whether the sample could skew the data before they trust the percentages.
apps.spoken: Her opinion might skew the poll since she asked only her friends.
apps.writing: Use skew when data, wording, or selection pushes a result away from the truth.

cloze.s: A survey given only at the gym will ___ the results toward people who already love exercise.

cloze2.s: Careless wording in a question can ___ the answers, because people respond to the tone as much as to the topic.

misuse.s: To skew the results fairly, the researchers surveyed every kind of student in equal numbers.
misuse.why: Skew means to distort results; surveying every kind of student equally prevents distortion.

visual.alt: A bar chart leaning to one side as if pushed.

words.frame: Leaving out ___ could skew the picture because ___.

words.def: Choosing only certain items from a larger group, often leaving others out.
words.ex: The documentary was selective: it showed only the days when the river was flooded.
words.ex2: Being selective about sources should mean choosing reliable ones, not ones that agree with you.
words.nonExample: Including every important fact, even the ones you dislike, is not selective.

apps.academic: A selective use of evidence quotes only the lines that support a claim and passes over the rest.
apps.spoken: You're being selective; you only mentioned the good reviews.
apps.writing: Use selective to criticize a report that picks facts to fit a side; use thorough for the opposite.

cloze.s: The lawyer's ___ quotations made the witness sound angry, though most of the interview had been calm.

cloze2.s: Because the guidebook was ___, it described the famous beaches and said nothing about the crowds.

misuse.s: A selective report includes every relevant fact, whether it helps the writer's side or not.
misuse.why: Selective means picking only some facts; including every fact is the opposite.

visual.alt: A hand picking a few cherries from a full basket.

words.frame: The writer was selective when he ___ but left out ___.

words.def: Loyalty and support for a person, group, cause, or country.
words.ex: The captain's allegiance was to the whole team, not just to her close friends.
words.ex2: New citizens are often asked to promise allegiance to the country's constitution.
words.nonExample: Switching sides every time a different group offers you something is not allegiance.

apps.academic: A writer's allegiance to a political group can shape which facts appear in an article.
apps.spoken: My allegiance is to my town's team, even when they lose.
apps.writing: Use allegiance for strong, lasting loyalty, especially to a group, cause, or nation.

cloze.s: Her ___ to the school's rival was so strong that she refused to cheer when our team scored.

cloze2.s: Long after he moved away, he kept his ___ to the small town where he grew up.

misuse.s: The spy showed great allegiance by secretly selling her country's plans to its enemy.
misuse.why: Allegiance means loyalty; selling plans to an enemy is betrayal.

visual.alt: Two people shaking hands in front of a flag.

words.def: The way a person notices and understands something, shaped by senses and experience.
words.ex: A person's perception of a speech can change with the clothes the speaker wears and the lights on the stage.
words.ex2: Her perception of the neighborhood changed after she walked through it at sunrise.
words.nonExample: A measurement such as the height of a doorway is a fact, not a matter of perception.
words.rel: how things appear to a person

apps.academic: A photograph can shape the public's perception of an event even when it shows only one corner of it.
apps.spoken: My perception is that the class got louder after lunch, but I haven't counted.
apps.writing: Use perception for how something seems to a person, and separate it from the facts that can be checked.

cloze.s: The photograph shaped the public's ___ of the event, though it showed only one corner of the crowd.

cloze2.s: Two witnesses can see the same accident, yet each person's ___ of what happened may differ.

misuse.s: Perception means a fact that is exactly the same for every person in every situation.
misuse.why: Perception depends on the person who notices; a fact the same for everyone is not a perception.

visual.alt: An eye linked by an arrow to a thinking brain.

words.def: To control or influence a person or situation in a clever, unfair, or dishonest way.

senses.def: To handle or move something skillfully, usually with the hands.
senses.example: The surgeon manipulated the tiny tool with steady fingers.

words.ex: Some ads manipulate viewers by showing happy families while hiding the product's flaws.
words.ex2: He tried to manipulate his sister into doing his chores by pretending to be sick.
words.nonExample: Explaining your idea honestly and letting a friend decide is not manipulating.

apps.academic: Propaganda tries to manipulate emotions so that people stop asking for evidence.
apps.spoken: Don't let a countdown timer manipulate you into buying something you don't need.
apps.writing: Use manipulate for unfair control of people; use handle or operate for physical objects.

cloze.s: The scammer tried to ___ the grandmother's trust by pretending to be her grandson.

cloze2.s: Cropping the photograph can ___ how viewers feel about the crowd, making a small group look huge.

misuse.s: A good teacher manipulates students by telling them the whole truth and letting them decide.
misuse.why: Manipulate suggests unfair control; telling the whole truth and letting people decide is the opposite.

visual.alt: A puppeteer's hands pulling strings attached to a small figure.

words.frame: An ad can manipulate people by ___.

words.def: Causing strong disagreement or debate among many people.
words.ex: The decision to cut the arts program was controversial, and the meeting ran past midnight.
words.ex2: A controversial statue can divide a town long after the artist has explained it.
words.nonExample: A rule that every member of the community happily supports is not controversial.

morph.note: The final y of controversy changes to i before -al.

apps.academic: When a topic is controversial, a fair report names more than one side and says who holds each view.
apps.spoken: I know it's controversial, but here is why I support it.
apps.writing: Use controversial for topics and decisions that divide people; avoid it for ideas that are merely unusual.

cloze.s: The new dress code was so ___ that students wrote letters, parents emailed the principal, and the board held two extra meetings.

cloze2.s: Because the topic was ___, the teacher asked everyone to name a source before speaking.

misuse.s: The proposal was controversial because every citizen agreed on it right away.
misuse.why: Controversial means causing debate; instant agreement is the opposite.

visual.alt: Speech bubbles clashing above a crowd of people.

words.frame: The topic is controversial because some people ___ while others ___.

words.def: To leave something out, whether on purpose or by mistake.
words.ex: The editor omitted the second half of the senator's sentence, which changed its meaning.
words.ex2: Please do not omit your sources when you turn in the research paper.
words.nonExample: Printing every line of an interview, including the parts you dislike, does not leave anything out.

apps.academic: An omission can be as powerful as a false statement, because readers cannot judge what they never see.
apps.spoken: You omitted the part where you started the argument.
apps.writing: Use omit when a detail is missing from an account, and ask whether it was left out by accident or on purpose.

cloze.s: A careful historian will not ___ evidence that contradicts her theory.

cloze2.s: The recipe card ___ a key step, so the first batch of cookies never rose.

misuse.s: The student omitted three paragraphs by adding them to the end of her essay.
misuse.why: To omit is to leave out; adding paragraphs is the opposite.

visual.alt: A page with a gap where a line has been cut out.

words.frame: The writer omitted ___, which changes the story because ___.

passage.title: Two Reports, One Vote
paras: When the school board voted on whether to replace the old library with a robotics lab, two reports about the meeting appeared by Friday. Ms. Alvarado asked her media class to read both and decide what each one was trying to do.

The first report came from the Falcon Flyer, a newsletter run by the robotics club. Its headline was "Board Backs the Future," and its first three paragraphs quoted only students who wanted the lab. Nadia noticed the slant right away. "The vote was controversial," she said, "but this reads like a victory lap."

The second report, on a neighborhood blog, leaned just as far in the other direction. Its author belonged to a partisan group of residents who wanted the library saved, and the post accused the board of "bulldozing childhood." Marcus pointed out that neither writer had lied. "They are both selective," he said. "Each one picked the facts that fit a side and left the rest alone."

Ms. Alvarado asked the class to look for what each report had omitted. The Flyer never mentioned that the lab would cost more than the board first estimated. The blog never mentioned that the old library's roof leaked in every storm. "Leaving out one fact can skew the whole picture," she said, "even when every sentence you did write is true."

Then she asked about motive. "Every writer has an agenda, even if it is only wanting you to keep reading. The question is whether the agenda is open or hidden." Priya added that the blog writer's allegiance to the neighborhood was obvious in the first line, while the Flyer pretended to be neutral. "That makes the Flyer better at manipulating readers," she said, "because you cannot see it happening."

By the end of class, the students agreed that perception depends on the sources you choose to read. Their assignment was to write a third report that treated both sides fairly, and Nadia's first sentence was already on the board: "Not everyone agrees on what a library is for."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, Nadia says the Flyer has a "slant." Which meaning of slant fits her use?
choices: a sloping line in the newsletter's design
a presentation that leans toward one side
a mistake in the quotations
a list of statistics about the vote
qs.why: Nadia says the report "reads like a victory lap" after quoting only supporters, so slant means a one-sided way of presenting information.

qs.q: Why does Marcus say that both writers are selective even though neither one lied?
choices: Each one included only the facts that supported a side.
Each one wrote too little about the vote.
Each one copied sentences from the other report.
Each one was unsure which facts were true.
qs.why: He says each writer picked facts that fit a side and left the rest, which is selective even when every statement is true.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the Flyer omitted a fact that matters?
choices: Its headline was "Board Backs the Future."
It was run by the robotics club.
It never mentioned that the lab would cost more than the board first estimated.
Its first three paragraphs quoted students.
qs.why: The missing cost increase is a relevant fact that the report leaves out; the other details describe what the report did include.

qs.q: Why does Priya think the Flyer may be better at manipulating readers than the blog is?
choices: The Flyer has more readers than the blog does.
The Flyer's headline is longer and more detailed.
The Flyer hides its agenda by pretending to be neutral, so readers cannot see the influence.
The blog never mentions a cost or a vote.
qs.why: Priya says that because the Flyer pretends to be neutral, readers cannot see what it is doing; the blog's allegiance is obvious.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Student newsletters should never report on school board votes.
A true report can still give a distorted picture when facts are chosen or left out.
Robotics labs are more useful than libraries.
Readers should trust a blog more than a newsletter.
qs.why: Ms. Alvarado explains that leaving out a fact can skew the picture even when every sentence is true, and both reports do this.

write.prompt: Think of a news story, ad, or social media post you have seen. Explain what its slant was and what it omitted, using at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: The source had a slant toward ___. It was selective when ___, and it omitted ___, so readers might ___.

study.task: Choose one word from the unit and build its family with the endings above, such as manipulate, manipulation, and manipulative, or partisan and partisanship. Say how the ending changes the part of speech and the meaning, and then use two family words in a sentence about a news story.

choices: loyal : disloyal
author : book

sentences: Write a sentence about a news story, ad, or video that has a slant. Name what it favors.
Write a sentence that uses both omit and skew to show how a missing fact changes a result.
Write a sentence about a person whose allegiance to a group makes them partisan.

given: The blog quoted only supporters of the library.
The blog skipped the leaking roof.
combine.model: Because the blog quoted only supporters and omitted the leaking roof, readers received a one-sided, skewed picture.

given: The ad never showed the high price.
The ad wanted people to buy quickly.
combine.model: The ad tried to manipulate viewers by showing smiling families, omitting the high price, and rushing them to buy quickly.

discuss: Is it possible for a report to be completely free of slant? Explain with slant and selective.
When is an omission an honest choice, and when is it a way to skew a story? Use omit and agenda.
How does your perception of a news story change when you learn who wrote it and why?
produce.explain: Explain the difference between a source that is partisan and a source that is simply wrong. Use partisan and one example.

argue.prompt: Claim: Social media sites should label posts that come from groups with a clear agenda. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A post with a hidden agenda could skew ___, but a labeled post would ___.

constructed.prompt: A travel brochure shows sunny beaches and quiet streets but never mentions the three-hour traffic jam to reach them. Use selective and omit to evaluate the brochure.
look: names what the brochure includes and what it leaves out
explains how the choice affects a reader's decision
constructed.model: The brochure is selective because it shows only the pleasant sights. It omits the traffic jam, so a reader may decide to visit without knowing the hardest part of the trip.

constructed.prompt: A website about a city election is run by the cousin of one candidate. Use agenda, allegiance, and partisan to explain why a reader should check its claims against another source.
look: connects the cousin's loyalty to a possible one-sided presentation
recommends a concrete way to check the claims
constructed.model: The writer's allegiance to a relative may give the site a hidden agenda, which makes it partisan. A reader should compare the site's claims with a report from a source that is not tied to either candidate.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for evaluating who is speaking and what they have chosen to show, read a short narrative about a media class comparing two reports on one school board vote, practice the endings -ive, -al, -ation, and -ship, and write an evaluation of a real source. The key habit is to ask what was included, what was left out, and who benefits.

notes.va.slant.n: Slant here is a lean toward one side, not a physical tilt, though the physical meaning is a good bridge (a tilted table makes everything roll one way). Ask students to find the loaded verb in a headline. Slant is not the same as lying: a slanted report can be accurate and still unfair.
notes.va.partisan.adj: Partisan means loyal to one side and unfair to others, often in politics but also in sports or any rivalry. Avoid linking it to a specific party. Practice with a sports example first so students feel the meaning before applying it to news.
notes.va.agenda.n: Many students know agenda as a meeting list or a planner. Teach both senses side by side, then focus on the motive sense. Have students ask what agenda an ad has, and accept honest purposes (informing) as well as hidden ones (selling).
notes.va.skew.v: Skew works for data and for stories: a biased sample skews a survey, and a missing fact skews a picture. Use a quick class poll taken only from the first row to show a skewed sample. English learners may confuse skew with skewer; point out the different spelling and meaning.
notes.va.selective.adj: Selective is neutral in everyday English (a selective college, a selective eater) but critical here when facts are chosen to fit a side. Pair with thorough as its opposite. Ask 'selective in what way?' to make students name what was picked and what was left.
notes.va.allegiance.n: Allegiance is lasting loyalty, stronger than liking. It can be positive (loyalty to a team) or lead to bias (loyalty that blinds). Avoid political examples that put students on the spot; use schools, teams, or families. Compare with loyalty and betrayal.
notes.va.perception.n: Perception is how something seems to a person, which can differ from the fact. Use an optical illusion or two people describing one photo. Keep the distinction with perceptive (g6) clear: perceptive is a trait; perception is the result.
notes.va.manipulate.v: Manipulate has a physical sense (handle skillfully) and an unfair-influence sense; teach the second and mention the first. Stress the unfair or hidden quality: explaining honestly is not manipulating. Use ads, countdown timers, and cropped photos as concrete examples.
notes.va.controversial.adj: Controversial means many people disagree. Model the suffix: controversy + -al. Students may use it for anything shocking or unusual; ask 'who disagrees with whom?' to check that the topic is truly divisive. Choose school-appropriate examples.
notes.va.omit.v: Omit is leaving out, on purpose or by mistake. The chosen examples show that an omission can mislead without a false word. Practice by cutting one sentence from a paragraph and asking how the meaning changes. Remind students that the spelling doubles the t in omitted.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'This newsletter quotes only supporters, so it is selective. It never mentions the higher cost, so it omitted a fact that matters. Every sentence could be true and the picture could still be skewed. Now I ask what agenda the robotics club might have, and I decide the slant is mild but real.'
discuss: Which is worse for a reader: a false statement or an important omission? Defend your choice.
How could a writer with a strong allegiance still try to be fair?
misconceptions: A biased source must contain lies.
Perception is always wrong, while facts are always clear.
extend: Find two articles on the same topic from different sources and chart what each includes, omits, and implies.
Rewrite a slanted headline three ways: neutral, supportive, and critical. Explain which words changed.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Bring back slant, selective, and omit within two days when students read any news, social media, or history source, and again at one week in a short written evaluation. The grade 8 words ambiguous, implicit, and nuance return as tools for describing what a slanted source suggests without saying.

frames: The source has a slant toward ___ because it ___.
The writer was selective when ___, and omitted ___.
I think the agenda is ___ because ___.

wida.oral: Partner A reads two headlines about the same event. Partner B names which one has a slant, points to a word that shows it, and says what the other headline omits.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: sesgo (slant), partidista (partisan), propósito (agenda; Spanish agenda usually means a planner or calendar, so the false-friend risk should be taught), sesgar (skew), lealtad (allegiance).
Cognate flags for selectivo, percepción, manipular, controvertido, and omitir should be confirmed; controvertido and polémico are both common in Spanish.
Sense boundaries: slant, agenda, skew, and manipulate each carry a second everyday sense shown on the word card; the unit teaches only the evaluative sense in the passage.
